questions.question: Why is the product rule not simply $(fg)' = f'g'$?
options: Only the derivative of the first factor contributes.
Only the derivative of the second factor contributes.
The derivative is $f'(x)g'(x)$ when both factors are nonconstant.
questions.explanation: Changing either factor changes the product, producing the two terms $f'g+fg'$.
questions.polish_notes: Reworded MCQ stem to ask the mathematical question directly rather than referring to a choice/option.; Replaced overly obvious distractors with closer misconceptions; Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: The product rule $(fg)'(x)=f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x)$ adds a term for each factor's variation; keeping only $f'g$ accounts for varying $f$ while leaving $g$ fixed, so the term $fg'$ — the change due to varying $g$ with $f$ fixed — never appears.

Both factors vary, so $(fg)'(x)=f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x)$ has two terms; retaining only $fg'$ captures the variation of $g$ (with $f$ fixed) and discards $f'g$, the contribution from varying $f$ while $g$ stays fixed.
Even for nonconstant factors, $f'g'$ misses both undifferentiated factors.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
